questions.question: Which description fits an algorithm for solving a problem?
options: A single formula that gives the answer directly from the data
A prescribed sequence of computational rules to solve the problem
A mathematical model stating the objective and the constraints
Trying values by intuition until one of them seems good enough

questions.question: Two analysts apply the same algorithm, whose rules and tie-breaks are fully prescribed, to the same data and start from the same initial solution. Must they obtain the same output?
options: No, since an iterative method makes a free choice in each iteration
Yes, since every step is fixed by the prescribed rules
Only if the algorithm is exact rather than a heuristic
Only if both analysts carry out the same number of iterations

questions.question: Two solution procedures for the same optimization model both always return an allowed plan. What distinguishes a heuristic among them?
options: It has no general guarantee that its plan is optimal
It always needs fewer iterations than an exact method
It may return plans that violate some of the constraints
It applies its rules only once instead of repeatedly

questions.question: A search starts with the interval $[0,64]$. Each iteration keeps one half of the current interval, so its length halves, and the method stops as soon as the length is at most 1. How many iterations are carried out?
options: 7 iterations
5 iterations
6 iterations
64 iterations

questions.question: A planner uses this procedure: start at the depot; repeat "travel to the nearest town not yet visited" until every town has been visited; then return to the depot. Which part is the stopping condition?
options: Every town has now been visited once
Travel to the nearest unvisited town
The start of the route at the depot
The total distance of the final route

questions.question: A procedure starts with $x=1$ and doubles $x$ in each iteration. Which stopping condition would never be met, so that the procedure would run for ever?
options: Stop when $x\ge100$
Stop when $x>50$
Stop when $x=100$
Stop when $x=64$

questions.question: During an iterative optimization method, one iteration produces a new solution with exactly the same objective value as before. What can be concluded?
options: The method has reached an optimal solution and should stop
The method has failed and must be restarted from a new solution
The new solution must violate at least one of the constraints
Nothing yet; iterations need not strictly improve the value

questions.question: The same improvement rule is run twice on one model, from two different starting plans, and stops with two different final values of the objective. What does this show about the rule?
options: Both final plans must be optimal, because both runs stopped
It does not always find the best value, so it is not exact
The rule has a programming error that needs correcting
The best value is the average of the two final values

questions.question: For whole $x$ from 0 to 6, $f(x)$ takes the values 4, 6, 5, 3, 2, 7, 1. Starting at $x=2$, a rule moves to the neighbour $x-1$ or $x+1$ with the lower $f$ if that is below the current value, and stops when neither neighbour is lower. Where does it stop?
options: At $x=4$
At $x=6$
At $x=3$
At $x=2$

questions.question: A model has exactly 20 allowed plans. A method starts at one of them, and each iteration moves to another allowed plan with a strictly better objective value. At most how many iterations can it carry out?
options: 19 iterations
20 iterations
No limit, as it may cycle
Just 1 iteration

questions.question: A new solution rule is tested on one instance of a model and returns the optimal plan there. Does this establish that the rule always returns an optimal plan?
options: Yes; one correct optimal answer proves the rule exact
Yes, provided the rule also needed few iterations
No; it would need a guarantee for every instance
No; it would need to succeed on at least two instances

questions.question: Does an iterative method that strictly improves its objective value in every iteration always meet its stopping condition after finitely many iterations?
options: Yes; strict improvement always ends the run after finitely many steps
Yes, as long as the objective values cannot go below some bound
No, but only because some iterations may not improve the objective
No; the improvements can shrink so that the stopping value is never reached

questions.question: For whole $x$ from 0 to 3, $f(x)$ takes the values 3, 2, 2, 5. A rule starts at $x=1$, moves to a neighbour whose $f$ is at most the current value (the left one first if both qualify), and stops when no neighbour qualifies. What happens?
options: It stops at $x=1$ at once, with $f=2$
It moves between $x=1$ and $x=2$ for ever
It stops at $x=2$ after one iteration
It stops back at $x=1$ after two iterations

questions.question: For whole $x\ge0$, a scan for the smallest value of $f(x)=x^2-9x+20$ starts at $x=0$; while $f(x+1)\le f(x)$ it sets $x$ to $x+1$, and it stops as soon as $f(x+1)>f(x)$, outputting $x$. Which $x$ does it output?
